area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: When a patient is cancelled from the trauma list, are they offered food or drink within 1 hour of the cancellation?
why: Patients fasted for a trauma list are often cancelled and then left nil by mouth for hours or into the next day, risking dehydration, delirium and acute kidney injury. Cancellations [2170] and pre-operative fasting (ONA-107) are audited; what happens after cancellation is not.

standard.wording: Patients cancelled from a theatre list are offered food or drink within 60 minutes of the decision to cancel.

pass: Documented offer of food or drink within 60 minutes of the recorded cancellation decision, in patients with no clinical reason to stay nil by mouth.
population: Adults fasted for the trauma list and cancelled for that day. Exclude patients kept nil by mouth for a clinical reason (e.g. bowel obstruction, unsafe swallow) and those still possible for a later list the same day.
sample: Every trauma list cancellation over 4 weeks (typically 20–40); extend until 30 cases.
data_source: Theatre cancellation log; coordinator call time; ward nursing notes and fluid/food chart.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Time the coordinator phones the ward

timeline: Wk 1–4 collect; Wk 5 analyse/present; Wk 6 change; Wk 7–12 embed; Wk 13–16 re-audit
change: Add a 'Cancelled: may eat and drink now?' step to the theatre coordinator's cancellation checklist; the coordinator phones the ward with a one-line script and records the time.
reaudit: Weeks 13–16: same template, next 4 weeks of cancellations.
close_loop: Present at the theatre users' group and trauma governance. If it worked, write the step into the trauma list standard operating procedure.
evidence: [2170] same-day theatre list cancellations: cancellation counts only, not what happened to the patient afterwards
ONA-107 (proposed): time from last clear drink to being sent for, on the trauma list
pitfalls: No time is recorded when a case is cancelled → agree before week 1 that the coordinator's phone call time is the start time, and put it on the checklist
Staff keep patients fasted 'in case they go later' → record 'later list still possible today' and count only definite cancellations
Ward nurses feel blamed → present it as a theatre-to-ward communication gap; show results by day of week, never by named ward or nurse
The fix fades when the audit team rotates → build it into the coordinator checklist, not a poster
pearls: Recruit the trauma coordinator and one ward sister in week 1; they collect the data and run the fix
Use a one-line script: '[Patient] is cancelled today and may eat and drink now'
Record next-day nil-by-mouth time as well; it is often the larger harm
Pilot on one ward for 2 weeks before rolling out; name the theatre matron as owner afterwards
Bring one patient story (e.g. 30 hours without food) to governance alongside the percentages
effort: ~10 min per 5 cases from the cancellation log and ward charts

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: On elective orthopaedic lists, what proportion of turnarounds take 15 minutes or less?
why: Turnaround is lost theatre time between cases. The only turnaround audit in the corpus is a baseline with a mean of 37.7 minutes against a 15-minute target [2768]; no closed-loop turnaround audit exists in orthopaedics.

standard.source: Local standard; 15-minute turnaround target as used in [2792]
standard.wording: Turnaround (patient leaves theatre to start of the next patient's anaesthetic) of 15 minutes or less.

pass: Time from one patient leaving theatre to the start of the next patient's anaesthetic is 15 minutes or less.
population: All turnarounds on elective orthopaedic lists. Exclude the last case of each list (no following case).
sample: Every turnaround on elective orthopaedic lists over 4 weeks (typically 80–150), plus the previous 4 weeks from the theatre system as a baseline.
data_source: Theatre management system timestamps; delay reason recorded by the theatre coordinator.
timeline: Wk 1–4 collect; Wk 5 analyse/present; Wk 6 change; Wk 7–12 embed; Wk 13–16 re-audit
change: Make 'send for next patient' a fixed step on the theatre checklist, triggered at the start of wound closure and time-logged by the coordinator. If the delay data point elsewhere, fix the leading delay reason instead.
target: ≥50% of turnarounds within 15 minutes and median reduced by 10 minutes
reaudit: Weeks 13–16: same template, 4 weeks of lists.
close_loop: Present the weekly median and top three delay reasons at the theatre users' group. If it worked, add turnaround to the monthly theatre dashboard owned by the theatre manager.
evidence: [2768] Northern Ireland: mean turnaround 37.7 min against a 15-min target; cleaning 8.1 min, extubation 5.1 min (baseline only)
[2379] UK emergency theatre: turnover 39 → 11 min after a dedicated theatre registrar separate from on-call
[2366] UK golden patient policy: first-case start times 30 min earlier on average
[1236] UK elective orthopaedics: presenting at governance alone left team-brief start at 08:05 → 08:08
pitfalls: Theatre-system times are entered late or missing → spot-check 10 cases against a stopwatch before week 1; hand-collect week 1 if they differ
'Orthopaedic turnaround is longer because of laminar flow and big trays' → report median by procedure type (joints, hands, trauma), not one overall figure
Staff speed up only while watched → use 4 weeks of past theatre-system data as a hidden baseline
Nurses and ODPs hear 'work faster' → involve the theatre manager from day 1 and frame it as removing waits (porters, beds, trays)
pearls: Record a delay reason for every turnaround; it tells you which fix to use
Find the list that already turns around fastest and copy its routine
Convert minutes to cases: 20 min saved × 3 turnarounds ≈ one extra case a day
Book the porter for the send-for time, not 'when free'
Take one chart to governance: weekly median turnaround with a line where the change went in
effort: ~2 hours to export and clean 4 weeks of theatre-system data

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: On elective orthopaedic lists, what percentage of the planned session time is touch time?
why: Touch time utilisation is the national productivity measure, but a single percentage hides where time is lost; the corpus has no orthopaedic audit of it.

standard.source: GIRFT touchtime utilisation target, as reported in PMC11488670 (CC BY)
standard.wording: The Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) programme has set targets to achieve 85% touchtime utilisation by 2024/25. Touchtime utilisation is a measure of theatre productivity, defined as the time from the start of anaesthesia to the time a patient leaves the theatre for all cases on a defined theatre list as a percentage of total available theatre time.

pass: List touch time (start of anaesthesia to leaving theatre, summed over all cases, within the planned session) is 85% or more of planned session time.
population: All elective orthopaedic lists. Exclude lists cancelled in full.
sample: All elective orthopaedic lists over 4 weeks (one row per list).
data_source: Theatre management system session and case timestamps.

template.note: First anaesthetic start minus session start

timeline: Wk 1–4 collect; Wk 5 analyse/present; Wk 6 change; Wk 7–12 embed; Wk 13–16 re-audit
change: Fix the largest single source of lost time found: usually the first-case start, using a golden patient (first case identified and prepared the day before).
reaudit: Weeks 13–16: same template, 4 weeks of lists.
close_loop: Present lost minutes by cause at the theatre users' group; if it worked, embed the fix in list-planning procedure and track on the theatre dashboard.
evidence: [2366] UK golden patient policy: start times 30 min earlier on average
[1236] UK elective orthopaedics: average team-brief start 08:05 → 08:08 after governance presentation only
pitfalls: The percentage rewards overrunning or under-booked lists → report late start, turnaround and early finish minutes alongside it
Session times in the system differ from real contracted times → confirm planned session length with the theatre manager before week 1
Surgeons dispute the data → share the raw list-by-list sheet with each team before presenting
pearls: Break lost time into late start, turnarounds and early finish; the fix follows the biggest bar
Pair with the turnaround audit and share one data export
Report cases gained, not percentages, to managers
effort: ~2 hours to export and clean 4 weeks of theatre-system data

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: In elective hip and knee replacements, what percentage of theatre waste by weight goes into the orange (infectious) waste stream?
why: Arthroplasty produces about 14 kg of waste per case, most of it sent to the infectious stream for high-temperature treatment, although much is packaging or non-infectious [1738].

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 14
standard.wording: RECYCLE/use lowest carbon appropriate waste streams: use recycling waste streams for packaging or, if not available, domestic waste stream (prior to patient entering the room); use non-infectious offensive waste streams (yellow/black tiger) unless clear risk of infection (orange); ensure only appropriate contents in sharps bins (sharps/drugs)

pass: Per case: orange-stream waste as a percentage of total theatre waste weight. Local target: orange share halved from cycle 1.
population: Elective primary total hip and knee replacements. Exclude revisions for infection and patients with known transmissible infection.
data_source: Bag weights recorded by the scrub or circulating team at the end of each case; theatre system for procedure details.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4–8 set up with estates; Wk 9–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Place tiger (offensive) and recycling bins in every arthroplasty theatre; open packaging into recycling before the patient enters; keep the orange bin for items with a clear infection risk, as defined in writing with infection prevention.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: same template, next 20 consecutive cases.
close_loop: Present kilograms, cost and carbon per case at theatre users' group and the Trust sustainability group. If it worked, add the bins to the theatre set-up standard and roll out to all orthopaedic theatres.
evidence: [1738] UK multicentre arthroplasty: 14.79 kg per THA and 13.61 kg per TKA; infectious waste 9.88 kg and 8.68 kg; only 5 of 10 trusts had an offensive stream
[2552] UK theatres: recycling 18.4% → 36.7%, falling back to 26.4% the next month (quick guide only)
[2668] UK general surgery: recyclable share 17% → 28% with posters, but total waste per case rose
pitfalls: Infection prevention objects to moving waste out of orange → agree a written rule for what stays orange before week 1 and quote Green Theatre Checklist item 14
The waste contract has no offensive stream → involve the estates waste manager in week 1; the change date depends on the contract
No scales in theatre → borrow a hanging scale from estates or the waste contractor; weigh each bag before it is tied off
Gains fade after the launch [2552] → make the bins part of the fixed theatre layout, not a poster campaign
Total waste rises while the orange share falls [2668] → report total kg per case alongside the percentage
pearls: Recruit the scrub lead and the estates waste manager as co-leads
Open all packaging into recycling before the patient enters, so nothing is contaminated
Photograph a typical orange bag at baseline; it persuades faster than numbers
Convert kg to cost and carbon using the contractor's price per tonne for each stream
Name a green champion for each theatre to keep the bins in place after rotation
effort: ~5 min per case to weigh bags; 1 hour to analyse

area: Orthopaedic perioperative, theatre and ward care
question: On primary knee replacement instrument trays, what proportion of the instruments are used during the operation?
why: Every instrument on a tray is washed and sterilised whether used or not; trays carry instruments that are rarely touched [2671].

standard.source: Intercollegiate Green Theatre Checklist v2.0 (November 2024), item 9
standard.wording: REVIEW AND RATIONALISE: clarify necessary kit for case and specify what should be available to open only if needed: “Just in time”; take the opportunity to review instrument sets and identify any targets for overage reduction

pass: Per instrument: used in at least 10% of cases. Instruments used in under 10% of cases are candidates for removal to a separate 'open if needed' pack.
population: Primary total knee replacements using the standard tray. Exclude revisions.
data_source: Tray list ticked by the scrub practitioner at the end of each case (instrument handed or used = used).
timeline: Wk 1–3 collect; Wk 4 analyse/present; Wk 5–10 agree new tray with surgeons and sterile services; Wk 11–14 embed; Wk 15–17 re-audit
change: Remove instruments used in under 10% of cases from the main tray into a separate 'open if needed' pack, agreed with all knee surgeons and sterile services.
target: ≥80% of tray instruments used per case
reaudit: Weeks 15–17: same template, 20 cases on the new tray; record any 'open if needed' pack openings.
close_loop: Present instruments removed, sterilisation cost and carbon saved at the arthroplasty meeting. If it worked, update the sterile services tray list and review hip trays next.
evidence: [2671] UK laparoscopic cholecystectomy: 7–19 of 63 tray instruments used; new tray with 60% fewer instruments
pitfalls: Surgeons fear a missing instrument mid-case → keep every removed item in a sealed 'open if needed' pack in the theatre
Surgeons use different instruments → count per surgeon and remove only items unused by all
Sterile services cannot change tray lists quickly → involve the sterile services manager from week 1
pearls: Have the scrub practitioner tick the tray list during closure, while it is fresh
Show surgeons the list of never-used instruments with their names on it; agreement follows quickly
Count 'open if needed' pack openings in the re-audit to prove safety
effort: ~3 min per case for the scrub practitioner
